newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hoping bedroom brouhaha will blow over.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hoping bedroom brouhaha will blow over.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and his battle-worn staff believe the Lincoln Bedroom brouhaha will blow over and scoff at any notion the fund-raising furore behind it equals great White House scandals of years past.
But Republican critics are determined to make this controversy stick to Clinton in a way past flaps have not.

With tales of rich campaign contributors being treated like royalty in the White House, the controversy is generating screaming headlines, hourly television updates, perky soundbites from political pundits and demands for investigation by members of Congress.

In the eye of the storm is Clinton. He is trying to carve out a historical legacy for himself on improving education and balancing the budget, but is struggling to explain why he had big-money donors to the Democratic Party stay overnight in the White House -- and, in particular, the glamorous Lincoln Bedroom, associated with American icon Abraham Lincoln.

"I don't think people who support you and help you through tough times and who believe in what you're doing should be disqualified from being the president's guests at the White House," Clinton said in his most recent public defence.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry says the affair is "a hot story" that will run out of steam.
"I don't know how long (it will last), but it clearly will be in the short term," McCurry said.

He dismissed any comparison with the Iran-contra scandal that marred President Ronald Reagan's second term, in which White House aides secretly sold arms to Iran and funnelled profits to Nicaragua's contra rebels in defiance of U.S. law.
"I don't believe that's an accurate comparison. There were specific allegations of wrongdoing that were pursued in Iran-contra," McCurry said.
Added another White House official who spoke on condition of anonymity: "I think it'll blow over. There's not much there ... We disclosed everything, it's gone."

But Republicans whose party was devastated by the Watergate scandal that drove President Richard Nixon out of office in 1974 are in a state of outrage. Their demands for an independent counsel to investigate the affair so far have been rejected by Clinton's attorney general, Janet Reno.
But the flap is bound to come up in congressional hearings into other allegations involving campaign fund-raising, such as whether the Chinese government steered money to Democrats.

"Abraham Lincoln would be turning over in his grave if he knew the Lincoln Bedroom was being rented out to bolster a candidate's political agenda," said California Republican Representative Wally Herger.

Former Republican President George Bush, Clinton's predecessor, went out of his way to keep the Clinton White House from trying to accuse him of also inviting the rich and famous to overnights in the White House.
His office in Houston, Texas, released a list of 273 people who stayed overnight in the White House during his tenure, and there were few major fundraisers.
Of Clinton's 831 named guests, by contrast, about a third made campaign donations in 1995 and 1996, and some generated hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Bush's former press secretary, Marlin Fitzwater, said he believed the evidence was clear that Clinton made some decisions based on the desires of fat-cat contributors -- an allegation the White House hotly denies.

"What President Clinton has done," Fitzwater said, "is put in the minds of the public a specific price on the presidency, on himself and on his decisions. I don't know any modern presidency where that's ever happened."

Democrats say Republicans share the blame for the special access they give to big-money donors, such as an event last week in Florida where some were invited to rub shoulders with House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott.
Democratic consultant Jennifer Laszlo noted that polls put campaign finance reform low on the public's priorities list.

"I don't believe they think Bill Clinton is any more for sale than Newt Gingrich or Trent Lott or any other politician is, because I think Americans at this point think almost all politicians are corrupt," Laszlo said.
But Republicans say the issue upsets people in a way other controversies -- such as the Clintons' Whitewater investment and a sexual harrassment suit against Clinton -- have not.
"Whitewater didn't cut, but the Lincoln Bedroom ticks them off," said Republican pollster Frank Luntz.
